'''Judith Sharn Young''' ({{Nee|'''Rubin'''}}; September 15, 1952 – May 23, 2014)<ref name=":0" /> was an American [[physicist]], astronomer,<ref name="Larsen 1928">{{cite web |last=Larsen |first=Kristine |date=December 31, 1999 |title=Vera Cooper Rubin |url=http://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/rubin-vera-cooper |access-date=July 1, 2016 |website=Shalvi/Hyman Encyclopedia of Jewish Women |publisher=[[Jewish Women's Archive]] |archive-date=July 24, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160724213319/http://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/rubin-vera-cooper |url-status=live }}</ref> and educator. The [[American Physical Society]] honored Young with the first [[Maria Goeppert-Mayer Award]] for being the best young physicist in the world in 1986.<ref name="Oakes 2007 p. 792">{{cite book |last=Oakes |first=E.H. |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uPRB-OED1bcC&pg=PA792 |title=Encyclopedia of World Scientists |publisher=[[Facts On File]] |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-4381-1882-6 |series=Facts on File Science Library |page=792 |language=en |chapter=Young, Judith Sharn |access-date=July 1, 2016}}</ref><ref name="APS Physics | APS Home 2016">{{cite web |date=July 1, 2016 |title=Maria Goeppert Mayer Award |url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/awards/goeppert-mayer.cfm |access-date=July 1, 2016 |website=[[American Physical Society]] |archive-date=August 9, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180809111423/https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/awards/goeppert-mayer.cfm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="UMass Amherst 2014">{{cite web |date=May 28, 2014 |title=Obituary: Judy Young, Astronomer Who Built Campus Sunwheel |url=http://www.umass.edu/newsoffice/article/obituary-judy-young-astronomer-who-built |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160818135526/http://www.umass.edu/newsoffice/article/obituary-judy-young-astronomer-who-built |archive-date=August 18, 2016 |access-date=July 1, 2016 |website=[[University of Massachusetts Amherst]]}}</ref> Astronomer [[Nick Scoville]] of [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] writes of her research: "Her pioneering galactic structure research included some of the earliest mapping of CO emission in galaxies followed by the most extensive surveys [of] molecular gas and star formation in nearby galaxies."<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Scoville |first1=Nick |author-link=Nick Scoville |last2=Schneider |first2=Steve |date=January 31, 2014 |title=Judith S. Young (1952–2014) |url=https://baas.aas.org/pub/judith-s-young-1952-2014/release/1 |journal=[[Bulletin of the AAS]] |language=en |publisher=[[American Astronomical Society]] |volume=46 |issue=1 |page=007 |bibcode=2014BAAS...46..007S |bibcode-access=free |access-date=September 17, 2023 |archive-date=September 7, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220907184507/https://baas.aas.org/pub/judith-s-young-1952-2014/release/1 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Career ==
Young received her Bachelor of Arts degree in Astronomy from [[Harvard University]] and graduated with Honors.<ref name="UMass Amherst 2014" /><ref name=":3" /> She received her M.S. and Ph.D. in physics from the [[University of Minnesota]].<ref name=":3" />

Young began a postdoctoral fellowship at [[University of Massachusetts|UMass]] in 1979, collaborating with [[Nick Scoville|Nick Z. Scoville]] in a study which measured the cold gas and [[carbon monoxide]] content of [[Galaxy|galaxies]].<ref name="UMass Amherst 2014" /> The pair made the discovery that the distribution of light and gas is proportional in galaxies.<ref name="UMass Amherst 2014" /> The [[American Astronomical Society]] awarded her the [[Annie Jump Cannon Award in Astronomy|Annie J. Cannon Prize]] for this work in 1982.<ref name="Oakes 2007 p. 792" /><ref name="UMass Amherst 2014" />

Young became an assistant professor at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]] in 1985.<ref name="UMass Amherst 2014" /> In 1989, Young was promoted to associate professor with tenure, and became a Full Professor in 1993.<ref name="UMass Amherst 2014" /> She published more than 130 papers, mentored 5 Ph.D. candidates, and supervised 15 undergraduate research projects.<ref name=":3" />

Young is perhaps best known for her Sunwheel project.<ref name=":2">{{Cite magazine |last=Mackenzie |first=Dana |date=January-February 2000 |title=A Megalith for the Millennium |url=https://www.americanscientist.org/article/a-megalith-for-the-millennium |url-status= |website=[[American Scientist]] |volume=88 |issue=1 |pages=23–24 |issn=0003-0996 |jstor=27857959 |archive-url= |archive-date= |access-date=September 17, 2023}}{{deadlink|date=September 2023}}</ref> Young's goal for this project was to bring astronomy down to earth and to an empty lot behind the football stadium at the UMass-[[Amherst College|Amherst]] campus.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> In addition to her academic work, Young volunteered on the UMass campus and in her local community.<ref name="UMass Amherst 2014" /><ref name=":3" />

== Personal life ==
Young was born in Washington, D.C., the daughter of astronomer [[Vera Rubin]] and mathematical biophysicist [[Robert Joshua Rubin]], and sister to mathematician [[Karl Rubin]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Vera Rubin |url=http://gruber.yale.edu/cosmology/vera-rubin |access-date=December 26, 2016 |website=[[The Gruber Foundation]] |publisher=[[Yale University]] |archive-date=May 9, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509192422/https://gruber.yale.edu/cosmology/vera-rubin |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/02/04/AR2008020403043.html|title=Robert J. Rubin, 81; Scientist Whose Work Combined Disciplines|last=Sullivan|first=Patricia|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=February 5, 2008|access-date=October 26, 2018|language=en-US|issn=0190-8286|archive-date=June 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190621060049/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/02/04/AR2008020403043.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

She was married to Michael Young from 1975 to 1990<ref name=":0">
{{Cite book |last=Gardner |first=Sue Ann |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780313293030/ |title=Notable Women in the Physical Sciences: A Biographical Dictionary |publisher=[[Greenwood Press]] |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-31-329303-0 |editor-last=Shearer |editor-first=Benjamin F. |location=Westport, CT |pages=438–443 |language=en |chapter=Judith Sharn Young |editor-last2=Shearer |editor-first2=Barbara S. |chapter-url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/libraryscience/115/}}</ref> and had a daughter, Laura.<ref name="APS Physics &#124; APS Home 2016" />

Judith Young died from complications resulting from [[multiple myeloma]], a disease she lived with for eight years.<ref name="APS Physics &#124; APS Home 2016" /><ref name=":3" />
